beset.gloss: To trouble or harass someone from every side at once; in older use, to surround or hem something in.

senses.head: Trouble from every side
senses.body: The living sense, and almost always passive — *beset by* delays, *beset with* problems. The trouble is the subject and the person or project it surrounds is the object.
examples: Small delays *beset* every large construction job.
Doubts *beset* her the whole night before the interview.
The expedition *has been beset* by bad weather since Tuesday.
By March the project *had been beset* with lawsuits.

senses.head: Surround, hem in
senses.body: The literal military sense — attackers closing in on all sides. Literary and largely archaic; modern American English says *surround* or *besiege*.
examples: Wolves *beset* the camp on three sides that winter.
The travelers *had been beset* by bandits before they reached the pass.

senses.head: Stud, set thickly with
senses.body: Very rare and poetic: a surface *beset with* jewels. You will meet it only in older texts and in translations that keep an old flavor.
examples: A crown *beset* with rubies lay on the cushion.
The binding *has been beset* with small pearls along the spine.

bet.gloss: To risk money on an outcome, or, in everyday speech, to say you are fairly sure of something.

senses.head: Wager money on an outcome
senses.ru: делать ставку, ставить деньги, биться об заклад
senses.body: The core sense: *bet* an amount *on* something, or *bet someone* that something will happen. American English keeps *bet* in the past and participle where British writing sometimes allows *betted*.
examples: I never *bet* more than I can afford to lose.
He *bet* twenty dollars on the Sunday game and lost it.
She *has bet* on that same horse three years running.

senses.head: I bet — I'm fairly sure
senses.body: Present tense even though it is the same shape as the past, and nearly always first person. Conversational, and often ironic — *I bet you did*.
examples: I *bet* she's stuck in traffic again.
I'll *bet* he never even read the memo.

senses.head: You bet — certainly
senses.ru: конечно, ещё бы; не за что
senses.body: A fixed spoken reply meaning “yes, definitely,” and across much of the U.S. also a casual “you're welcome.” Speech only.
examples: “Can you cover Friday?” “*You bet*.”
“Thanks for the ride.” “*You bet*.”

senses.head: Bet on — rely on
senses.body: Figurative: to treat an outcome as safe enough to plan around. Very often negative — *don't bet on it*, *I wouldn't bet on him*.
examples: Don't *bet* on the weather holding through Sunday.
The whole plan *had bet* on interest rates staying low.

broadcast.gloss: To send a program or signal out over radio, television, or the internet; more loosely, to tell something to everyone.

senses.head: Transmit a program
senses.body: The main sense, for radio, TV, and streaming alike. Edited American prose keeps *broadcast* in all three slots; *broadcasted* is common in speech but most editors still change it.
examples: The station *broadcasts* the local news at six.
NPR *broadcast* the hearings live all day Thursday.
That episode *has been broadcast* in forty countries.

senses.head: Announce to everyone
senses.body: Figurative and usually disapproving — spreading something widely that should have stayed private.
examples: Please don't *broadcast* my phone number to the whole office.
He *broadcast* the news before the family had been told.

senses.head: Scatter seed by hand
senses.body: The original agricultural sense — throwing seed widely instead of sowing it in rows — and the source of the radio meaning. Still current among farmers and gardeners.
examples: We *broadcast* clover seed across the pasture in March.
The mix *had been broadcast* over the bare ground before the rain.

burst.gloss: To break open suddenly under pressure, or to move or act with sudden force.

senses.head: Break open under pressure
senses.body: Of pipes, balloons, tires, dams — anything that gives way all at once. There is no *bursted*, so the time word carries the tense.
examples: Balloons *burst* if you fill them too far.
Water pipes *burst* all over the city during the freeze last January.
Two of the tires *have burst* since we bought the trailer.

senses.head: Burst into — move suddenly
senses.body: Sudden, forceful movement into or out of a place; the preposition carries the direction.
examples: She *burst* into the room without knocking.
Three kids *had burst* out of the building before the alarm stopped.

senses.head: Burst into tears or flames
senses.body: A fixed frame for something that starts all at once, with a noun after *into*. *Burst into tears*, *burst into flames*, and *burst into song* are the common ones.
examples: He *burst* into tears in the middle of the ceremony.
That model *has burst* into flames twice on the highway.

senses.head: Burst out laughing / crying
senses.body: The same idea with an -ing verb instead of a noun. *Burst out* also introduces sudden speech: *“Enough!” he burst out*.
examples: He *bursts* out laughing every time he hears that song.
She *burst* out crying before she got through the first sentence.

senses.head: Be bursting with — overflowing
senses.body: Progressive only, and usually figurative — bursting with pride, energy, or news. A closet can be *bursting with* clothes as well.
examples: The closets are *bursting* with things nobody uses.
He was *bursting* with news about the promotion.

senses.head: Be bursting to do something
senses.body: Informal, progressive only, and always with an infinitive: barely able to hold back from doing something.
examples: She was *bursting* to tell someone the whole time.
I am *bursting* to ask him what really happened.

bust.gloss: Informal: to break something, to raid or arrest, or to reduce someone in rank. Everyday American usage prefers the regular *busted*.

senses.head: Break, smash
senses.body: Informal for *break*. American English usually says *busted* in the past and participle; the invariant *bust* sounds British or old-fashioned. In writing that matters, use *broke*.
examples: Don't *bust* the lock — I have a key somewhere.
He *bust* his ankle skateboarding last summer.
Two of the hinges *had bust* clean off before we noticed.
My brother *busted* his phone screen again.

senses.head: Raid or arrest (police)
senses.body: Slang from law enforcement and crime reporting: police *bust* a club, or *bust* someone *for* something. Write *raided* or *arrested* in formal prose.
examples: Vice *has bust* that club twice this year.
He got *busted* for driving without a license.

senses.head: Demote in rank
senses.body: Military and police usage, usually passive: *he was busted to private*. Always regular here.
examples: The colonel *busted* him to private for the stunt.
Two sergeants *have been busted* since the investigation opened.

senses.head: Bust up — break apart, brawl
senses.body: *Bust up* a fight, a marriage, or the furniture; intransitively, a couple *busts up*. Informal throughout.
examples: They *busted up* over money after eleven years.
Somebody *had busted up* the picnic tables during the night.

senses.head: Bust a gut, bust chops
senses.ru: надрываться, из кожи вон лезть; придираться, пилить
senses.body: Set slangy phrases: *bust a gut* is to work or laugh very hard, and *bust someone's chops* is to nag or needle them.
examples: He *busted* a gut getting the truck loaded before dark.
Don't *bust* my chops about the deadline — I know.

cast.gloss: To throw or send something out, to choose actors for parts, or to shape molten metal in a mold.

senses.head: Choose actors for parts
senses.ru: распределять роли, проводить кастинг, утверждать на роль
senses.body: The commonest modern sense: *cast someone as* a character, or *cast* a film as a whole. Never *casted* in edited prose — *casted* survives only as shop talk inside the industry.
examples: They *have cast* an unknown actor as the lead.
The director *had cast* the whole film before the script was finished.
She *casts* mostly out of open auditions.

senses.head: Throw, cast a line
senses.body: The old literal sense, alive in fishing (*cast a line*) and in writing with a formal flavor. Ordinary speech says *throw*.
examples: She *cast* the line into the shallow water and waited.
Learn to *cast* into the wind and you can fish anywhere.

senses.head: Cast a vote or ballot
senses.body: The fixed phrase for voting; *cast a ballot* and *cast a vote* are equally standard, and the news writes little else.
examples: Voters *cast* their ballots on Tuesday.
More than a million people *have cast* early votes this cycle.

senses.head: Cast light, a shadow, doubt
senses.body: A frame for whatever a thing projects, literal or figurative: *cast a shadow*, *cast light on the problem*, *cast doubt on a claim*.
examples: The lamp *casts* a long shadow across the hallway.
The audit *has cast* doubt on every figure in the report.

senses.head: Cast a glance or eye
senses.body: A slightly formal way of saying *look*. Common in writing, rare in speech.
examples: He *cast* a quick glance at the door and kept talking.
Would you *cast* an eye over these numbers before I send them?

senses.head: Cast blame or suspicion
senses.body: To direct blame, suspicion, or aspersions at someone. Formal, and a staple of reporting on scandals.
examples: Don't *cast* the blame on people who weren't in the room.
The memo *had cast* suspicion on the wrong department.

senses.head: Cast a spell
senses.body: Fixed in magic and fantasy — *cast a spell on someone*. The figurative use follows easily: a place can *cast a spell over* you.
examples: The witch *casts* a spell that turns the prince to stone.
That coastline *has cast* a spell over painters for a century.

senses.head: Cast metal in a mold
senses.body: The foundry sense, and the source of *cast iron* and a plaster *cast*. Usually passive, and the participle often works as an adjective.
examples: The bell *was cast* in a foundry outside Cincinnati.
They *cast* the replacement part in bronze last month.

senses.head: Cast off / cast aside
senses.body: *Cast off* is to untie a boat and, in knitting, to finish the last row; *cast aside* is to discard something or someone. Both are on the formal side.
examples: We *cast* off at dawn and were out of the harbor by six.
He *had cast* aside every draft before the good one came.

senses.head: Cast about / around for
senses.ru: искать, подыскивать, ломать голову в поисках
senses.body: To search for something intangible — an idea, an excuse, a replacement. Literary rather than spoken.
examples: She *cast* about for a polite way to say no.
The committee *has cast* around for a new chair since March.

clear-cut.gloss: To log an area of forest by taking every tree at once.

senses.head: Log every tree at once
senses.ru: вырубать лес сплошь, вести сплошную рубку
senses.body: A forestry term, and the only verb sense there is. The far commoner adjective *clear-cut* — *a clear-cut case of fraud* — is a separate word and never behaves like this verb.
examples: The company *clear-cuts* about a thousand acres a year.
Loggers *clear-cut* that ridge back in the 1970s.
Half the watershed *has been clear-cut* since the mill reopened.
The slope *had been clear-cut* long before the state bought it.
They plan to *clear-cut* the northern parcel next spring.

cost.gloss: To have a particular price, or to make someone lose something.

senses.head: Have a price
senses.body: The core sense, invariant in all three forms: *the repair cost four hundred dollars*. Never *costed* here.
examples: A ticket *costs* about ninety dollars now.
Good tools *cost* money, but they last.
The repair *cost* more than the car was worth.
Rent *has cost* us more every year since we moved in.

senses.head: Make someone lose something
senses.body: The thing lost is the object and the person is the indirect object: *it cost him the promotion*. Money is not involved.
examples: That one mistake *has cost* us two customers already.
His temper *cost* him the promotion last year.

senses.head: Take effort or sacrifice
senses.body: Of effort rather than price: *it cost her a great deal to say that*. Slightly formal, and the object is usually an amount of pain or trouble.
examples: It *cost* her more than she let on to walk away.
Speaking up in that meeting *had cost* him every ally he had.

senses.head: Cost a fortune
senses.ru: стоить целое состояние, влететь в копеечку
senses.body: Fixed informal phrases for something expensive. *That'll cost you* is a joking price attached to a favor.
examples: Parking downtown *costs* an arm and a leg on game days.
Getting the roof fixed *cost* us an arm and a leg.

senses.head: Work out a price (costed)
senses.body: The one sense that is regular — *costed*, never invariant *cost*. Accounting and contracting writing only.
examples: The contractor *costed* the job at twelve thousand dollars.
We *have costed* out both options and the second is cheaper.

crosscut.gloss: To cut across something — across the grain of a board, or between two scenes on film.

senses.head: Saw across the grain
senses.ru: пилить поперёк волокон, делать поперечный распил
senses.body: Woodworking. A crosscut goes across the grain; ripping goes along it, and the tool for the first is a *crosscut saw*.
examples: You *crosscut* the board first, then rip it to width.
He *crosscut* the plank a quarter inch too short.
This blade *crosscuts* cleanly but tears the grain when you rip.

senses.head: Alternate two scenes on film
senses.body: Editing vocabulary, interchangeable with *intercut*. Usually *crosscut between* two lines of action.
examples: The editor *has crosscut* between the two conversations.
The director *had crosscut* the chase with shots of the empty house.

senses.head: Cut across, run counter to
senses.body: Academic and policy writing, usually about loyalties or categories that ignore the usual dividing lines. The -ing form does most of the work — *crosscutting concerns*, *crosscutting cleavages*.
examples: These loyalties *crosscut* every party line in the region.
The survey *had crosscut* the usual age brackets on purpose.

cut.gloss: To divide or wound with something sharp, to reduce an amount, and, in a long list of fixed phrases, to stop, shorten, or remove.

senses.head: Divide with a blade
senses.body: The literal sense — knife, scissors, saw. Usually with a phrase saying how: *cut it into slices*, *cut it in half*. Never *cutted*.
examples: Please *cut* the bread into thick slices.
She *cut* the rope with a pocketknife.
Someone *has cut* the cake already.

senses.head: Wound with something sharp
senses.body: Transitive and often reflexive, with a body part as object: *I cut my finger*. The participle doubles as an adjective — *a cut lip*.
examples: I *cut* my finger on the lid this morning.
He *had cut* his hand on the broken glass before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Reduce an amount
senses.body: Of budgets, prices, staff, taxes, and emissions. One of the most common verbs in business and political news.
examples: Airlines *cut* fares whenever a new route opens.
The state *cut* funding before anyone was told.
They *have cut* the budget twice since June.

senses.head: Cut hair
senses.body: *Cut someone's hair*, or, for what you had done to you, the passive — *I got my hair cut*.
examples: She *cuts* everyone's hair in the family.
He *cut* his own hair during the lockdown and it showed.

senses.head: Shorten, trim down
senses.body: Taking material out of something: *cut a scene*, *cut two pages*, *cut a trip short*.
examples: We *cut* the trip short because of the storm.
The editor *has cut* the chapter down to four pages.

senses.head: Skip class or work
senses.body: American school and workplace slang: *cut class*, *cut school*, *cut a shift*. British English says *skive*.
examples: He *cut* class three times last week.
Nobody *has cut* a shift since the new schedule went up.

senses.head: Cut off — interrupt, disconnect, isolate
senses.body: Three related uses: interrupting a speaker, ending a supply, and leaving a place unreachable. *Cut someone off* in traffic is a fourth.
examples: She *cut* me off before I finished the sentence.
The storm *had cut* off the whole valley by morning.

senses.head: Cut out — stop, remove
senses.body: *Cut it out* means stop that; *cut out* a picture is to remove it; an engine that *cuts out* dies suddenly.
examples: *Cut* it out — people are trying to sleep.
The motor *cut* out halfway across the lake.
They *have cut* two songs out of the set list.

senses.head: Cut down (on) — reduce; fell
senses.body: *Cut down on* something is to consume less of it; *cut down* a tree is to fell it. The object decides which you mean.
examples: I *have cut* down on coffee since the checkup.
They *cut* down the old maple last fall.

senses.head: Cut in — interrupt, overtake
senses.body: *Cut in line*, *cut in* on a conversation, or *cut in* on a car. Separately, *cut someone in* on a deal is to give them a share.
examples: A pickup *cut* in front of us on the ramp.
Somebody *has cut* in line ahead of forty people.

senses.head: Cut a deal or check
senses.ru: заключить сделку; выписать чек; записать пластинку
senses.body: Fixed American phrases where *cut* simply means make. *Cut a check* is standard business usage for issuing a payment.
examples: The two sides *cut* a deal an hour before the deadline.
Accounting *has cut* the check already.

downcast.gloss: To turn the eyes downward, or to dishearten someone. Literary and rare as a verb; the adjective *downcast* is what you normally meet.

senses.head: Lower the eyes
senses.body: The eyes or the gaze are almost the only possible object. In practice the participle-adjective carries the meaning — *downcast eyes* — and the verb itself is archaic.
examples: She *has downcast* her eyes every time the subject comes up.
He *had downcast* his gaze before the judge finished speaking.

senses.head: Dishearten, depress
senses.body: Literary and old-fashioned. Ordinary American English says *discourage* or *depress*.
examples: Long winters *downcast* the spirits of everyone on the island.
The news from the mill *downcast* the whole town that spring.
The verdict *downcast* everyone who had worked on the case.
Nothing *downcasts* a crew faster than a canceled contract.

english.gloss: To translate something into English. Rare, dated, and written with a small e to keep it apart from the name of the language.

senses.head: Translate into English
senses.body: A scholar's word, mostly historical — a royal committee *englished* the scriptures. Modern American English uses the regular *englished* when it uses the word at all, and normally just says *translated into English*. The *english* of pool and billiards, meaning spin on the ball, is an unrelated noun.
examples: Only a handful of scholars *english* Old Norse sagas today.
It is hard to *english* a joke that depends on grammar.
In 1611 a royal committee *englished* the Hebrew scriptures.
Nobody *has englished* that poet's late work yet.
By 1700 printers *had englished* most of the popular French romances.

fit.gloss: To be the right size or shape for something, to make something the right size, or to suit and belong.

senses.head: Be the right size
senses.body: The core sense, and the one that keeps the invariant *fit* in the American past and participle: *the jacket fit me perfectly last year*.
examples: These jeans *fit* better than the last pair.
The key *fit* the lock on the first try.
Nothing in that closet *has fit* me since high school.

senses.head: Suit, be consistent with
senses.body: Figurative: a story *fits* the facts, a person *fits* the job, a punishment *fits* the crime.
examples: That story *fits* everything else we know.
The description *fit* the man they arrested.

senses.head: Go into a space
senses.body: Intransitive, usually with *in*, *into*, or *through*: *will it fit in the trunk?*
examples: Six people *fit* in that car if nobody has luggage.
The couch *had fit* through the door on the way in, somehow.

senses.head: Install, equip with
senses.body: Regular in American English — *fitted*, not invariant *fit*: *the room was fitted with sprinklers*. British English prefers *fitted* for every sense.
examples: They *fitted* the whole floor with new smoke alarms.
The van *has been fitted* with a lift.

senses.head: Tailor or measure someone
senses.body: Also regular: *the tailor fitted the jacket*, *the optician fitted her for lenses*. The person, not the garment, is often the object.
examples: The tailor *fitted* the jacket in twenty minutes.
She *has been fitted* for a brace twice this year.

senses.head: Fit in — belong among people
senses.body: Of a person among people: *he never fit in at that school*. American English allows the invariant *fit* here; *fitted in* sounds British.
examples: He never *fit* in at that school.
New hires *fit* in faster when someone shows them around.

senses.head: Fit someone in (schedule)
senses.body: Of appointments and errands squeezed into a full day: *can the doctor fit me in Thursday?*
examples: The dentist *fit* me in at four.
She *has fit* two more meetings into an already full day.

forecast.gloss: To say what is likely to happen, especially with weather, money, or demand.

senses.head: Predict the weather
senses.body: The everyday sense, and usually passive when the forecaster is not named: *rain is forecast for Thursday*.
examples: The service *forecasts* snow above five thousand feet.
Rain was *forecast* for Thursday afternoon.
The bureau *had forecast* clear skies for the whole weekend.

senses.head: Project a business figure
senses.body: Finance and planning: analysts *forecast* growth, companies *forecast* demand. *Forecasted* turns up here and is not flatly wrong, but *forecast* is safer in edited prose.
examples: We *forecast* demand from three years of sales data.
Analysts *forecast* a slowdown months before it arrived.
Nobody *has forecast* a swing this large.

senses.head: Foretell, foreshadow
senses.body: A non-technical, slightly formal use in which an event itself *forecasts* what follows. Less common than *foreshadow*.
examples: The early strikes *forecast* a long and bitter winter.
Nothing in the data *had forecast* the collapse.

hit.gloss: To strike something, to reach a level or a place, or to arrive somewhere suddenly and do damage.

senses.head: Strike with force
senses.body: The core sense, with a hand or an object: *hit someone*, *hit the ball*, *hit the wall*. Never *hitted*.
examples: Don't *hit* your brother.
He *hit* the ball over the fence in the second inning.
The car *has hit* that same post twice.

senses.head: Collide with, crash into
senses.body: Of vehicles and moving things. The victim usually appears in the passive — *she was hit by a car*.
examples: A truck *hit* the guardrail and rolled.
Two deer *have been hit* on that stretch this month.

senses.head: Reach a level or number
senses.body: Prices, temperatures, populations, and milestones all *hit* figures. Very common in news writing.
examples: Gas prices *have hit* five dollars a gallon.
The thermometer *hit* a hundred and four on Sunday.

senses.head: Strike an area or group
senses.body: Of something that arrives suddenly and does damage: a storm, a recession, a scandal.
examples: Storms *hit* that coast every fall.
The news *had hit* the wires before the family was told.

senses.head: Go to a place
senses.body: Casual American usage: *hit the gym*, *hit the store*, and *hit the road*, meaning leave.
examples: Let's *hit* the road before the traffic starts.
We *hit* three record stores in one afternoon.

senses.head: Occur to someone
senses.body: Of a realization arriving all at once. The thought is the subject and the person is the object: *it hit me that...*
examples: It *hit* me halfway home that I had left my laptop there.
The full cost *has* not *hit* him yet.

senses.head: Hit on — flirt; devise
senses.body: *Hit on an idea* is to think of it; *hit on someone* is to make a pass at them. Same words, very different registers, and only context separates them.
examples: She *hit* on a way to cut the wiring in half.
Somebody *had hit* on the same solution two years earlier.

senses.head: Hit it off — click
senses.body: Fixed phrase, always with *it*, and almost always about a first meeting.
examples: They *hit* it off at the wedding and married a year later.
The two departments *have* never *hit* it off.

senses.head: Hit up — contact, ask
senses.body: Informal and recent: *hit me up when you land*, *he hit his brother up for a loan*.
examples: *Hit* me up when you get in.
He *has hit* every friend he has up for money.

senses.head: Hit the brakes, the roof
senses.ru: ударить по тормозам; сесть за учёбу; взорваться от злости
senses.body: A family of fixed phrases where *hit* means start or go to. *Hit the roof* and *hit the ceiling* both mean lose your temper; *hit the sack* means go to bed.
examples: She *hit* the brakes and we all lurched forward.
My father *hit* the roof when he saw the bill.

hoist.gloss: To raise something heavy, usually with ropes, a crane, or a lot of effort.

senses.head: Raise with rope or crane
senses.body: The main sense, and regular in modern American English — *they hoisted the piano through the window*. The invariant *hoist* is an older participle.
examples: Two crew members *hoist* the mainsail every morning.
They *hoisted* the piano through a third-floor window.
By noon they *had hoisted* every crate onto the deck.

senses.head: Lift up bodily
senses.body: Everyday use for lifting something or someone with no machinery involved.
examples: She *hoists* her daughter onto her shoulders to see the parade.
He *hoisted* the duffel bag into the overhead bin.

senses.head: Raise a flag or banner
senses.body: Ceremonial and nautical: *hoist the colors*, *hoist the flag*. Usually passive when the thing stays up.
examples: They *hoist* the flag at sunrise and lower it at sunset.
The banner *has been hoisted* over the entrance since Friday.

senses.head: Hoist with one's own petard
senses.ru: попасть в собственную ловушку, угодить в свои же сети
senses.body: The one place the invariant *hoist* survives — from *Hamlet*, meaning blown up by your own bomb. A fixed phrase; do not rebuild it with other words.
examples: He was *hoist* with his own petard when the memo leaked.
The senator *has been hoist* with his own petard more than once.

hurt.gloss: To cause pain or damage, or to feel pain.

senses.head: Feel pain
senses.body: Intransitive, with the body part as subject: *my knee hurts*. There is no *hurted*, so the time word decides whether it is now or over.
examples: My shoulder *hurts* when it rains.
My knee *hurt* all week after the hike.
That tooth *has hurt* on and off since Christmas.

senses.head: Injure, cause physical pain
senses.body: Transitive and often reflexive: *I hurt my back*. The passive participle doubles as an adjective — *three people were hurt* means injured rather than forming a true passive.
examples: I *hurt* my back moving the couch on Saturday.
Nobody *has been hurt* at that intersection this year.

senses.head: Wound someone's feelings
senses.body: With a person or *feelings* as object. One of the commonest uses of the verb in ordinary speech.
examples: It *hurt* to hear her say that.
He never meant to *hurt* anyone.

senses.head: Damage, harm something
senses.body: Of reputations, chances, sales, and teams — the object is a thing rather than a body.
examples: The scandal *had hurt* the company long before the lawsuit.
Skipping practice *hurts* the whole team.

senses.head: It wouldn't hurt to
senses.body: A fixed negative frame for giving advice gently, and its cousin *it never hurt anyone*.
examples: It wouldn't *hurt* to call ahead and check.
A second opinion never *hurt* anybody.

senses.head: Be hurting — be struggling
senses.body: Informal and progressive only: an industry, a town, or a person short of money is *hurting*.
examples: Small farms are *hurting* after two dry summers.
He was *hurting* for cash until the check cleared.

input.gloss: To enter data into a computer or a system.

senses.head: Enter data
senses.body: The main sense. *Inputted* is widespread in computing and business writing, but *input* is what dictionaries list first, and *entered* or *typed in* usually reads better than either.
examples: Please *input* the account number before you hit save.
She *input* all four hundred records by hand last week.
Someone *has input* the wrong shipping address.
The clerk *had input* the figures twice by mistake.

senses.head: Feed into a process
senses.body: Engineering and modeling use: values, energy, or materials *input* to a system. The noun is usually the better choice — *the inputs to the model*.
examples: The sensor *inputs* a fresh reading every second.
Whatever you *input*, the model rounds it to two decimals.

inset.gloss: To set one thing inside another — a small map on a large one, a panel in a door.

senses.head: Place within a recess
senses.body: Building and craft work: shelves *inset* into a wall, stones *inset* in a ring. The participle is what you usually meet — *an inset panel*.
examples: The builder *inset* the shelves into the wall when he remodeled the kitchen.
The jeweler *had inset* three small stones along the band.

senses.head: Inset a map or picture
senses.body: Cartography and publishing. The noun — the small map in the corner — is stressed IN-set, while many speakers move the verb's stress to in-SET.
examples: Cartographers often *inset* a detail map in the lower corner.
This template *insets* the caption automatically.
A photograph of the author *has been inset* on the back cover.

intercut.gloss: To alternate shots from two different scenes in a film or video.

senses.head: Alternate two scenes in editing
senses.body: Film and video vocabulary, very close to *crosscut*. The frame is *intercut A with B* or *intercut between* two things.
examples: Editors often *intercut* an interview with archive footage.
She *intercut* the wedding scene with shots of the empty church.
In the 1962 version the editor *intercut* the trial with the riot outside.
The trailer *has been intercut* with clips from the sequel.

senses.head: Interleave, break up with
senses.body: Extended from the film sense to writing and performance — a narrative *intercut* with letters, a lecture *intercut* with jokes.
examples: The memoir *intercuts* the trial with scenes from her childhood.
He *had intercut* the two timelines so tightly that viewers lost track.

knit.gloss: To make cloth by looping yarn with needles, or, figuratively, to join and grow together.

senses.head: Knit with yarn and needles
senses.body: The literal craft sense, and the one American English makes regular — *she knitted a scarf*. The k is silent.
examples: She *knits* a sweater every winter.
They *knitted* hats for the shelter all last November.
He *has knitted* three blankets since he retired.

senses.head: Of bone: heal together
senses.body: Medical and everyday alike: a fracture *knits*. This sense keeps the invariant *knit*.
examples: The fracture *knit* faster than the doctor expected.
The bone *has knit* cleanly, so the cast comes off Friday.

senses.head: Knit one's brows
senses.body: A fixed phrase for frowning in thought or worry. Invariant *knit*, and rather literary.
examples: She *knits* her brows whenever the subject of money comes up.
He *had knit* his brows before I finished the question.

senses.head: Bind people closely together
senses.body: Figurative, and usually passive or adjectival — *a tightly knit family*, *a close-knit town*. Invariant *knit*.
examples: Grief *has knit* that family closer than anything else could.
It takes years to *knit* a group of strangers into a crew.

senses.head: Join parts into a whole
senses.body: Of arguments, regions, or organizations drawn together into one thing. Formal, and often *knit together*.
examples: The new rail line *knit* the two towns into one labor market.
She *had knit* the interviews together into a single narrative.

let.gloss: To allow something to happen, and, in a long list of fixed phrases, to release, admit, disappoint, or stop.

senses.head: Allow, permit
senses.body: The core sense, with a bare infinitive after the object: *let me go*, never ✗ *let me to go*. Never *letted*, and do not confuse it with *leave*.
examples: My parents never *let* me stay out past ten.
He *lets* the dog sleep on the couch.
They *have let* the lease run out.

senses.head: Let me, let's — propose
senses.body: *Let me* offers to do something; *let's*, a contraction of *let us*, proposes doing it together. The standard negative is *let's not*.
examples: *Let* me know when the package arrives.
*Let's* take the back road.

senses.head: Let go — release; fire
senses.body: Literally releasing your grip, figuratively giving up on something, and — as *let someone go* — the polite office word for firing them.
examples: *Let* go of the rope on three.
The company *has let* forty people go since January.

senses.head: Let in, let out
senses.body: Of doors, animals, and people. *Let out* also means end, for classes and shows — *school lets out at three*.
examples: Somebody *let* the dog out during the night.
She *had let* him in through the back before anyone saw.

senses.head: Let down — disappoint
senses.body: *Let someone down* is to fail them; literally, *let down* a hem or a rope is to lower it. The noun *letdown* comes from the first.
examples: He *let* the whole crew down and knew it.
The team *has* never *let* its fans down at home.

senses.head: Let off — excuse; set off
senses.body: *Let someone off* is to spare them punishment, *let off steam* is to vent, and *let off* fireworks is to set them off.
examples: The judge *let* him off with a fine.
Somebody *had let* off a firecracker in the hallway.

senses.head: Let up — ease off, stop
senses.body: Intransitive, of rain, pressure, pain, or effort: *the rain never let up*.
examples: The rain *let* up around four.
The pressure on the department *has* not *let* up all year.

senses.head: Let on — reveal, admit
senses.body: Informal, and usually negative: *don't let on that you know*.
examples: She never *let* on that she had already read it.
He *has* not *let* on how much the repair cost.

senses.head: Let alone — much less
senses.body: A fixed connector following a negative: *he can't walk, let alone run*. Separately, *let someone alone* means leave them in peace.
examples: I can't afford the rent, *let alone* a car payment.
*Let* him alone until he's finished.

senses.head: Let it slide or slip
senses.body: *Let it slide* is to overlook something, *let it slip* is to reveal it by accident, and *let it drop* is to stop discussing it.
examples: I *let* it slide the first two times.
He *had let* slip the date before the announcement.

senses.head: Rent out (British)
senses.body: British English for renting property out — *rooms to let*. American English says *rent*, though *sublet* is standard on both sides and comes from this sense.
examples: They *let* the upstairs flat to a student last autumn.
The cottage *has been let* every summer since 1990.

miscast.gloss: To give an actor a part that does not suit them, or to put a person or an issue in the wrong role.

senses.head: Miscast an actor
senses.ru: неправильно распределить роли, ошибиться с актёром
senses.body: Nearly always passive — *he was badly miscast as the villain*. Forms come from *cast*; *miscasted* is not standard.
examples: Directors *miscast* comic actors in serious parts all the time.
The studio *miscast* the lead and the film never recovered.
She *has been miscast* in every romantic comedy she has made.

senses.head: Put in the wrong role
senses.body: The figurative use outside the theater: giving a person a job or a public part that does not fit them.
examples: Making a shy manager the spokesman *miscasts* him completely.
He *had miscast* himself as a peacemaker and everyone knew it.

senses.head: Frame an issue wrongly
senses.ru: представлять в ложном свете, искажать суть
senses.body: Journalistic, close to *mischaracterize*: presenting something as the wrong kind of problem.
examples: The bill *has been miscast* as a tax increase.
Critics *miscast* the study as proof of something it never claimed.

misread.gloss: To read something wrong, or to misjudge a person or a situation. The past and participle keep the spelling but are said mis-RED.

senses.head: Read words incorrectly
senses.body: The literal sense — wrong time, wrong number, wrong word. Nothing on the page separates past from present; only the vowel does.
examples: I *misread* the departure time and missed the flight.
She *misreads* my handwriting every single time.
He *had misread* the label and used the wrong solvent.

senses.head: Misjudge a person or situation
senses.body: The commoner figurative sense: reading a mood, a market, or an intention wrong.
examples: People often *misread* politeness as agreement.
The market *has misread* the Fed twice this year.

senses.head: Misread an instrument or signal
senses.body: Technical: taking the wrong value off a gauge, a chart, or a test. Often the named cause in an incident report.
examples: The pilot *misread* the altimeter in the fog.
It is easy to *misread* a scale marked that finely.

offset.gloss: To balance one thing against another so that the two effects cancel out.

senses.head: Balance out, compensate for
senses.body: The everyday sense: a gain that cancels a loss. Forms follow *set*, so never *offsetted*.
examples: A federal credit *offsets* part of the cost.
Higher fuel prices *offset* most of the savings last quarter.
Rising rents *have offset* every raise she has gotten.

senses.head: Set one amount against another
senses.body: Bookkeeping and tax: *offset losses against gains*, *offset a debt*. The noun *offset* names the entry itself.
examples: You can *offset* capital losses against gains in the same year.
The refund *had offset* most of what she owed.

senses.head: Offset emissions
senses.body: Climate and corporate usage: paying for reductions elsewhere to cancel your own emissions. Almost always with *carbon* or *emissions*.
examples: The airline says it *offsets* every flight it sells.
The company *has offset* less than a tenth of what it emits.

senses.head: Place at a distance from
senses.body: Technical, in building, design, and typography: one element set off to the side of another. The participle-adjective is common — *an offset hinge*.
examples: *Offset* the second row of tiles by half a width.
The builder *had offset* the chimney a foot from center.

output.gloss: To produce something, especially data sent out by a machine or a program.

senses.head: Produce data or a file
senses.body: Computing use: a program *outputs* a file, a value, or an error. *Outputted* is common in programming writing, but keep *output* in edited prose.
examples: The script *outputs* a CSV file to the same folder.
Set the flag if you want the tool to *output* JSON instead.
The model *has output* the same error twice.

senses.head: Produce a quantity of goods
senses.body: Industry and economics: a plant, a mine, or a writer *outputs* a measurable amount. The noun is far commoner than the verb here.
examples: The old printer *output* three blank pages before it jammed.
By Friday the plant *had output* more units than in the whole prior month.

overstay.gloss: To stay somewhere longer than you were welcome or allowed to.

senses.head: Overstay one's welcome
senses.body: The commonest use, and nearly always with *welcome* as the object. Regular in real American English — write *overstayed*.
examples: Guests who *overstay* their welcome rarely notice it.
Nobody wants to *overstay* at a party that has clearly ended.
We *have overstayed* our welcome — let's go.

senses.head: Stay past a legal limit
senses.body: Immigration and parking: *overstay a visa*, *overstay the meter*. Always regular in this sense.
examples: He *overstayed* his visa by three months.
By August she *had overstayed* the ninety days her permit allowed.

proofread.gloss: To read a text closely to catch mistakes before it is published. The past and participle keep the spelling but are said PROOF-red.

senses.head: Check a text for errors
senses.body: The everyday sense — a last pass for typos, spelling, and punctuation rather than for content.
examples: She *proofreads* every contract before it goes out.
Would you *proofread* this paragraph for me?
I *proofread* the newsletter twice last night and still missed a typo.
The manuscript *has been proofread* by two editors.

senses.head: Read proofs against the copy
senses.body: The strict trade sense: comparing typeset proofs word by word against the edited manuscript. A proofreader does this; an editor does something else.
examples: He *had proofread* only half the galleys when the deadline passed.
Every page *has been proofread* against the marked-up copy.

put.gloss: To move something into a place or a position, and, by extension, to express, assign, or apply something.

senses.head: Place something somewhere
senses.body: The core sense, and it needs a place: *put the milk in the fridge*, not ✗ *put the milk*. Never *putted* — that belongs to golf's *putt*.
examples: *Put* the milk back in the refrigerator.
I *put* the keys on the counter an hour ago.
Someone *has put* my chair out in the hallway.

senses.head: Express in words
senses.body: Almost always with an adverb or a manner phrase: *to put it bluntly*, *how would you put it?*, *well put*.
examples: *Put* it in your own words and it will make more sense.
She *had put* the objection more politely than I would have.

senses.head: Assign a figure or blame
senses.body: The frame is *put X at* a number or *put X on* a person: *put the damage at two million*, *put the blame on the contractor*.
examples: Investigators *put* the damage at two million dollars.
Nobody *has put* a firm date on the opening yet.

senses.head: Put money or effort into
senses.body: *Put money into* a business, *put work into* a project, *put your heart into* something.
examples: They *put* forty thousand dollars into the renovation.
He *has put* years into that manuscript.

senses.head: Put a question to someone
senses.body: Formal: *put the motion to a vote*, *put the question to the committee*. Courtroom and debate talk adds *I put it to you that...*
examples: The chair *put* the motion to a vote.
The proposal *had been put* to the board twice already.

senses.head: Put on — wear, stage
senses.body: Four unrelated uses of one phrase: *put on a coat*, *put on ten pounds*, *put on a play*, and *put on an act*. *You're putting me on* means you're kidding me.
examples: *Put* on a jacket — it's colder than it looks.
The school *has put* on the same play three years running.

senses.head: Put off — postpone; repel
senses.body: *Put off* a meeting is to postpone it; something that *puts you off* disgusts or discourages you. The adjective *off-putting* comes from the second.
examples: We *put* the trip off until spring.
The smell *had put* half the class off lunch.

senses.head: Put up with — tolerate
senses.body: A fixed three-word phrasal verb; the object always follows the whole thing — *put up with the noise*, never ✗ *put the noise up with*.
examples: I *have put* up with that noise for two years.
She *put* up with a lot before she quit.

senses.head: Put out — extinguish; issue; inconvenience
senses.body: *Put out* a fire, *put out* a statement, or *put someone out*, meaning trouble them. As an adjective, *put out* means annoyed.
examples: Crews *put* the fire out before it reached the barn.
The company *has put* out three statements in two days.

senses.head: Put down — record, suppress
senses.body: Four uses that share nothing but the words: *put your name down*, *put down a rebellion*, *put a dog down*, and *put someone down*, meaning insult them.
examples: *Put* your name down on the list by the door.
They *had* to *put* the old dog down last spring.

senses.head: Put up — build; raise; accommodate
senses.body: *Put up* a building or a shelf, *put up* your hand, or *put someone up* for the night. *Put up a fight* means resist.
examples: They *put* up a new warehouse on the lot last year.
My aunt *has put* us up every summer since I was small.

senses.head: Put through — connect, endure
senses.ru: соединять (по телефону); заставить пройти через; оплачивать учёбу
senses.body: *Put a call through* is to connect it; *put someone through* something is to make them go through it; *put someone through school* is to pay for it.
examples: *Put* me through to the front desk, please.
She *has put* two kids through college on one salary.

quit.gloss: To stop doing something, to leave a job for good, or to close a program.

senses.head: Stop doing something
senses.body: Takes an -ing form, never an infinitive: *quit smoking*, not ✗*quit to smoke*. American English keeps *quit* in all three slots; *quitted* sounds British and dated.
examples: I *quit* eating sugar in January and lasted about six days.
You should *quit* checking your phone every two minutes.
She *has quit* trying to explain it to him.

senses.head: Leave a job, resign
senses.body: The commonest sense in daily American speech. *Quit on someone* adds the sense of abandoning them.
examples: She *quit* her job the week after the merger.
Three people *have quit* since the new manager arrived.
He *had quit* the team long before the season ended.

senses.head: Quit it, quit that
senses.body: A blunt spoken imperative, used to children or close friends. Rude from a stranger.
examples: *Quit* it — you're going to break something.
My mother told us to *quit* fighting in the back seat.

senses.head: Close a program
senses.body: Computing. On a Mac, *Quit* shuts the whole application down, while *close* only closes one window.
examples: *Quit* the app and open it again.
I *quit* Photoshop last night and the file was still locked this morning.
The installer won't run until you *have quit* every open program.

senses.head: Stop working, give out
senses.body: Informal, of engines, appliances, and body parts. Often *quit on someone*.
examples: The mower *quit* halfway through the yard.
My knees *have quit* on me since I turned fifty.

read.gloss: To take in written words, and by extension to interpret, to state, or to display information.

senses.head: Take in written words
senses.body: The core sense. The spelling never changes, but the past and participle are said /rɛd/, exactly like the color *red*.
examples: I *read* (REED) two newspapers every morning.
She *read* (RED) the whole novel on the flight to Chicago.
He *has read* that book three times.

senses.head: Read aloud to someone
senses.body: Frames: *read to someone*, *read someone something*, *read something back/out*.
examples: Would you *read* this paragraph back to me?
He *read* the kids a story every night that summer.
By the time we got there the clerk *had read* the whole list aloud.

senses.head: Interpret, make sense of
senses.body: Figurative: read a situation, a person's face, a map, a defense. *Read someone's mind* is fixed.
examples: A good pitcher *reads* the batter's stance.
She *read* the room and dropped the subject.
We *have read* the market wrong twice this year.

senses.head: Come across a certain way
senses.body: Intransitive, usually *read as* or *read like*: the impression a text or a person gives. No passive.
examples: That line *reads* as sarcastic in print.
The apology *read* as insincere to everyone who saw it.

senses.head: Say, state (of a text)
senses.body: Of a sign, label, or document — the wording is such-and-such. Takes no passive.
examples: The sign *reads* 'No entry after six.'
The original draft *read* differently on that point.
The plaque *had read* 'Founded 1902' before someone repainted it.

senses.head: Show or take a reading
senses.body: Works in both directions: the instrument *reads* a value, and a person *reads* the instrument.
examples: The gauge *reads* forty pounds.
The thermometer *read* ninety-eight at noon.
Someone from the utility *has read* the meter already.

senses.head: Retrieve data (computing)
senses.body: Of drives, scanners, and programs. The opposite operation is *write*.
examples: The drive *reads* discs but won't burn them.
The scanner *read* the barcode on the second try.
The program *has read* the whole file into memory.

senses.head: read up on
senses.body: Learn about a subject by reading, usually in preparation for something.
examples: I need to *read* up on the new tax rules.
She *read* up on the company the night before the interview.
He *has read* up on every treatment option there is.

senses.head: read into
senses.body: Find a meaning that may not be there. Usually negative: *don't read too much into it*.
examples: Don't *read* too much into a one-word answer.
The press *read* a threat into a fairly bland statement.

senses.head: Study a subject (British)
senses.body: British only, and formal even there: *read history at Cambridge*. Americans say *majored in*.
examples: She *read* law at Oxford in the eighties.
He *has read* classics for three years now.

rebroadcast.gloss: To broadcast something a second time, or to relay a signal onward.

senses.head: Air a program again
senses.body: Follows *broadcast*; *rebroadcasted* is not standard. In everyday speech Americans say *replay* or *air again*.
examples: The network plans to *rebroadcast* the finale on Sunday.
Public radio *rebroadcast* the interview the next morning.
The concert *has been rebroadcast* every December since 1998.

senses.head: Relay a signal onward
senses.body: Technical: a repeater or satellite picks up a signal and sends it out again.
examples: The tower *rebroadcasts* the signal to the far side of the valley.
The satellite *had rebroadcast* the feed to three continents before the outage.

recast.gloss: To replace an actor in a role, to rework something into a new form, or to melt and mold metal again.

senses.head: Cast an actor again
senses.body: Film and theater. Often passive — *the part was recast* — and never *recasted*.
examples: Producers *recast* the role after two weeks of shooting.
The part *has been recast* twice since the read-through.
They may *recast* the lead if she drops out.

senses.head: Rework into a new form
senses.body: Of an argument, a report, a policy: same material, different shape or framing.
examples: She *recasts* every complaint as a question.
He *had recast* the entire second act before opening night.
Let's *recast* this proposal in terms the board will understand.

senses.head: Melt down and mold again
senses.body: Metalworking, from *cast* in its foundry sense.
examples: The foundry *recast* the cracked bell in 1911.
The bronze *has been recast* three times over the centuries.

refit.gloss: To repair and re-equip something, especially a ship.

senses.head: Re-equip a ship or vehicle
senses.body: The home sense. American English normally uses the regular *refitted*; the invariant *refit* is mostly the noun, stressed REE-fit.
examples: The yard *refits* two ferries every winter.
They *refitted* the whole galley last spring.
The trawler *has been refitted* twice since it was launched.

senses.head: Re-equip a building or plant
senses.body: Chiefly British for shops and offices — *the store closed for a refit*. Americans say *remodel* or *renovate*.
examples: It would cost more to *refit* the old plant than to build a new one.
The chain *had refitted* forty stores before the money ran out.

senses.head: Put a part back on
senses.body: Mechanical and everyday: fit again something that was removed. *Refitted* is the normal form here.
examples: The mechanic *refitted* the panel and tightened every screw.
You will have to *refit* the door once the frame dries.

reread.gloss: To read something a second time, or to interpret a text in a new way.

senses.head: Read again
senses.body: Follows *read* down to the vowel trap: ree-REED in the present, ree-RED in the past and participle.
examples: I *reread* (ree-REED) my favorite novel every summer.
She *reread* (ree-RED) the email four times before answering.
He *has reread* the contract and still has questions.
They *had reread* the instructions twice and were still stuck.
It helps to *reread* a hard paragraph out loud.

senses.head: Reinterpret a text
senses.body: Academic and critical writing: read something again and come out with a different reading of it.
examples: Later critics *reread* the novel as a book about class, not romance.
Historians *have reread* the whole decade in light of those letters.

reset.gloss: To return something to its starting state, or to set it again to a new value.

senses.head: Return to the starting state
senses.body: The everyday sense, mostly of devices and accounts. Follows *set*, so never *resetted*.
examples: *Reset* the router and try again.
I *reset* my password twice this morning and still can't get in.
The technician *has reset* every machine on the floor.

senses.head: Set again to a new value
senses.body: Of clocks, counters, thermostats, and traps — set once more, not necessarily back to zero.
examples: Somebody *had reset* the clock an hour ahead.
This switch *resets* the counter to zero.
We need to *reset* the thermostat for the weekend.

senses.head: Start over, wipe the slate
senses.body: Figurative, common in politics and business. The noun is at least as common: *a reset in relations*.
examples: Both sides want to *reset* the relationship after the election.
The new coach *reset* expectations in his first week.

senses.head: Set a broken bone again
senses.body: Medical, and usually because the first attempt failed.
examples: The surgeon *reset* the wrist under anesthesia.
The break *had been reset* badly the first time.

retrofit.gloss: To add new equipment or systems to something that was built without them.

senses.head: Add equipment to an existing structure
senses.body: Engineering and construction. American writing strongly prefers the regular *retrofitted*.
examples: The city *retrofits* about a dozen schools a year.
They *retrofitted* the building with sprinklers in 2014.
Half the fleet *has been retrofitted* with cleaner engines.

senses.head: Adapt an old design after the fact
senses.body: Figurative, common in software: bolt a requirement onto a system that never anticipated it.
examples: It is cheaper to *retrofit* an old furnace than to replace it.
We *had retrofitted* the login system for two-factor before the audit.
Nobody wants to *retrofit* tests onto code this old.

rid.gloss: To free someone or something of something unwanted — almost always in *rid X of Y*, *get rid of*, or *be rid of*.

senses.head: get rid of
senses.body: By far the commonest use of the word, and the one learners need first. *Rid* here is the participle after *get*.
examples: I finally got *rid* of the old couch.
How do you get *rid* of fruit flies?
We got *rid* of almost everything in the garage last weekend.

senses.head: rid X of Y
senses.body: The full transitive frame, a shade formal. The reflexive *rid oneself of* is common in writing.
examples: Nothing will *rid* this basement of that smell.
The new manager *rid* the department of its worst habits.
He *had rid* himself of every reminder of the marriage.

senses.head: be rid of
senses.body: A state rather than an action: *get rid of* is the doing, *be rid of* is the result.
examples: I'm glad to be *rid* of that car.
She won't be *rid* of the paperwork until spring.

set.gloss: To place something deliberately, to fix a value or state, or (of the sun) to go down — one of the busiest verbs in English.

senses.head: Place something somewhere
senses.body: The core sense, and it always takes an object. *Sit* is the one without an object: you *sit* down, but you *set* something down. ✗*Set down and rest* is dialect.
examples: *Set* the box on the table by the door.
She *set* the tray down without a word.
They *had set* the table before the guests arrived.

senses.head: Fix a time, price, or setting
senses.body: Covers deadlines and prices as well as alarms, timers, and thermostats — anything given a value.
examples: The committee *has set* a deadline of March first.
The judge *set* bail at ten thousand dollars.
She *set* her alarm for five and still slept through it.
We need to *set* a price before Monday.

senses.head: Go down (of the sun)
senses.body: The one common sense with no object at all. The opposite is *rise*.
examples: The sun *set* behind the ridge around eight.
The moon *sets* before midnight this week.
The sun *had set* by the time we reached the trailhead.

senses.head: Become firm or solid
senses.body: Intransitive, of concrete, glue, jelly, and plaster.
examples: Let the concrete *set* overnight.
The gelatin *set* in about four hours.
The glue *has set*, so don't try to move it now.

senses.head: Establish a standard or record
senses.body: Fixed collocations: *set a record*, *set a precedent*, *set an example*, *set the tone*.
examples: She *set* a school record in the two hundred meter.
This decision *sets* a precedent nobody wants.
He *has set* the tone for the whole department.

senses.head: Place a story in a time or place
senses.ru: помещать действие (в определённое время или место)
senses.body: Nearly always passive: *the novel is set in 1930s Chicago*.
examples: The film *is set* in a small town in Maine.
They *had set* the whole play in a single room.

senses.head: Start someone or something going
senses.body: Frames: *set someone to work*, *set someone doing something*, *set something in motion*.
examples: The foreman *set* two crews to work on the roof.
That remark *set* me thinking.
The noise *has set* the dogs barking.

senses.head: set up
senses.body: Very common and broad: arrange, assemble, or establish something. It also means to frame someone: *I was set up*.
examples: Can you *set* up the projector before nine?
We *set* up the tent in the dark.
They *have set* up a fund for her medical bills.

senses.head: set off
senses.body: Three uses that share a shape: depart, trigger an alarm or reaction, and detonate something.
examples: They *set* off for the coast before dawn.
The smoke *set* off every alarm on the floor.
One comment *has set* off a week of arguing.

senses.head: set out
senses.body: Depart on a journey, state something in an orderly way, or lay items out. *Set out to do something* means to intend it.
examples: She *set* out to prove them all wrong.
The memo *sets* out three options.
He *had set* out the chairs an hour early.

senses.head: set back
senses.body: Delay progress, or — informally, always with a person and an amount — cost that much.
examples: The storm *set* the project back a month.
That repair *set* me back four hundred dollars.
Two recalls *have set* the company back years.

senses.head: set aside
senses.body: Reserve time or money, or — as a legal term — annul a verdict or ruling.
examples: *Set* aside an hour for questions.
We *set* aside money every month for the trip.
The appeals court *has set* aside the verdict.

shed.gloss: To let something fall away — leaves, hair, tears, weight, or a burden.

senses.head: Drop hair, skin, or leaves
senses.body: The literal sense, of animals and plants. No *shedded*.
examples: Our dog *sheds* year round.
The maples *shed* their leaves early that year.
That snake *has shed* twice this spring.

senses.head: Lose or get rid of
senses.body: Of weight, jobs, costs, doubts — anything a person or an organization drops on purpose.
examples: He *has shed* twenty pounds since January.
The company *shed* four hundred jobs last quarter.
She *had shed* the last of her doubts by the second interview.

senses.head: shed tears, shed blood
senses.body: Fixed and slightly formal. Often passive in the negative: *not a tear was shed*.
examples: They *shed* a few tears at the airport and then laughed about it.
Nobody wants to *shed* blood over a parking space.
Plenty of blood *had been shed* over that border already.

senses.head: shed light on
senses.body: Fixed idiom: make something clearer, usually a question or a mystery.
examples: The new emails *shed* light on who knew what.
Her testimony *has shed* light on a very murky deal.

senses.head: Repel water
senses.body: Of coatings, fabrics, and roofs: water runs off instead of soaking in.
examples: This jacket *sheds* rain but not wind.
The tarp *shed* water all night without leaking.

shit.gloss: To empty the bowels — vulgar — plus a handful of vulgar idioms built on the same verb.

senses.head: Empty the bowels
senses.body: Vulgar; keep it out of writing that matters. The past is genuinely unsettled — *shit*, *shat*, and *shitted* all occur, with *shit* commonest and *shat* usually played for laughs.
examples: The dog *shit* on the neighbor's lawn again last night.
Don't let the puppy *shit* in the house.
A raccoon *has shit* in the crawlspace.

senses.head: shit on someone
senses.body: Vulgar: treat someone with contempt, or badmouth them. Common in the passive.
examples: They *shit* on their own staff for years.
Nobody deserves to be *shit* on like that.
He *has shit* on every partner he ever had.

senses.head: shit oneself, shit a brick
senses.body: Vulgar fixed phrases for sudden terror. Rarely literal.
examples: I nearly *shit* myself when the alarm went off.
Half the office *had shit* a brick over the audit before anyone read the findings.

shred.gloss: To cut or tear something into strips, literally or figuratively.

senses.head: Cut into strips
senses.body: Ordinary American English treats this as a regular verb — *shredded* — even though dictionaries list the invariant form.
examples: *Shred* the cheese while the pasta boils.
He *shredded* every statement before recycling it.
The office *has shredded* six boxes of old files.

senses.head: Demolish an argument
senses.body: Figurative, of testimony, a theory, or a defense.
examples: The defense *shredded* the witness's timeline.
Her testimony *had shredded* the company's whole story by lunch.

senses.head: Come apart in strips
senses.body: Intransitive, of fabric, tires, and paper.
examples: The flag *had shredded* in the wind by the end of the week.
Cheap tires *shred* on gravel roads.

senses.head: Play or ride brilliantly
senses.body: American slang, from guitar solos and from skiing and skateboarding. Often intransitive.
examples: That kid can really *shred*.
They *shredded* the back bowls all afternoon.

shut.gloss: To move something into a closed position, and the base of several very common phrasal verbs.

senses.head: Close something
senses.body: Blunter than *close*, and it will not sit in front of a noun: *a closed door*, not ✗*a shut door*.
examples: Please *shut* the window — it's freezing.
He *shut* the door harder than he meant to.
She *shut* her eyes and counted to ten.

senses.head: Close for business
senses.body: Of stores, plants, and offices, temporarily or for good.
examples: They *have shut* the plant for two weeks of maintenance.
The diner *shuts* at nine on weeknights.
The store *had shut* by the time we got downtown.

senses.head: shut down
senses.body: Close an operation permanently, halt an activity, or power a machine off. Also of a person: *he shut down* means he stopped responding.
examples: The company *shut* down two plants last year.
*Shut* down the laptop before you unplug it.
Protests *have shut* down the interstate twice this month.

senses.head: shut off
senses.body: Stop a flow — water, gas, power — or cut something off from access.
examples: The city *shut* off the water at eight.
*Shut* off the burner when it starts to steam.
Somebody *had shut* off the alarm during the night.

senses.head: shut up
senses.body: Rude as an order. The second, older sense is to lock someone or something away: *shut up in a room*.
examples: He told them to *shut* up, which did not help.
She *shut* up the second her boss walked in.
The dog *had been shut* up in the garage all afternoon.

senses.head: shut out
senses.body: Keep something outside, exclude someone, or — in baseball and hockey — hold the other side scoreless.
examples: Heavy curtains *shut* out most of the street noise.
The rookie *shut* out the Yankees for seven innings.
New rules *have shut* small growers out of the market.

sight-read.gloss: To play or sing music from a score you have never seen before.

senses.head: Play music at first sight
senses.ru: играть или петь с листа (по нотам)
senses.body: Music only, and a real skill rather than a casual act. Follows *read* in pronunciation: the past and participle are said SITE-red.
examples: Good accompanists *sight-read* almost anything.
She *sight-read* the whole sonata at the audition.
He *has sight-read* for that choir for years.
They *had sight-read* the part once and then recorded it.
You have to practice to *sight-read* well.

simulcast.gloss: To carry the same program on two channels or media at the same time.

senses.head: Broadcast on two channels at once
senses.body: A blend of *simultaneous* and *broadcast*, and it inherits the invariance: never *simulcasted*.
examples: The station *simulcasts* the game on AM and FM.
They *simulcast* the ceremony on three platforms last May.
The network *had simulcast* the address in Spanish as well.

senses.head: Send a live event to other venues
senses.ru: транслировать в прямом эфире на другие площадки
senses.body: Common in horse racing, cinema, and corporate events: one live feed shown in many rooms at once.
examples: The track *simulcasts* races from six other venues.
The concert *has been simulcast* to theaters nationwide.
We plan to *simulcast* the keynote to every regional office.

slit.gloss: To make a long, narrow cut in something.

senses.head: Cut a long narrow opening
senses.body: One straight cut, not a break into pieces — that is *split*, one letter away.
examples: *Slit* the bag open along the top.
He *slit* the envelope with a kitchen knife.
Someone *has slit* the seam on this cushion.
This blade *slits* plastic wrap cleanly.

senses.head: Slit a throat or wrists
senses.body: Nearly fixed collocations, and the sense most people meet first: *slit someone's throat*, *slit his wrists*. Often passive.
examples: He threatened to *slit* the man's throat.
The animal's throat *had been slit* cleanly.

split.gloss: To break or divide something into parts, to share something out, or — in slang — to leave.

senses.head: Divide into parts, share out
senses.body: The commonest sense. No *splitted*, ever.
examples: Let's *split* the check.
We *split* the last piece of pie three ways.
That firm *splits* profits evenly among the partners.

senses.head: Break or crack along a line
senses.body: Works with or without an object. The -ing form as an adjective means severe: *a splitting headache*.
examples: He *split* a stack of firewood before breakfast.
The log *had split* along an old crack.
The seam *has split* on both sides.

senses.head: Divide into opposing groups
senses.body: Of parties, committees, congregations, and towns.
examples: The party *has split* into two camps.
The vote *split* the town down the middle.
A single issue can *split* a coalition in a week.

senses.head: split up
senses.body: End a relationship, or divide people into smaller groups.
examples: They *split* up after eleven years.
Let's *split* up and cover both entrances.
Two of my cousins *have split* up this year.

senses.head: Leave, take off
senses.body: Informal American slang, a little dated but still understood.
examples: We *split* around midnight.
He *had split* before the police arrived.

senses.head: split the difference
senses.body: Fixed phrase from bargaining: settle halfway between two numbers.
examples: We *split* the difference and settled at nine thousand.
They *have split* the difference on every contract so far.

senses.head: split hairs
senses.ru: придираться к мелочам, спорить о пустяках
senses.body: Fixed idiom, always critical: argue over distinctions too fine to matter.
examples: Don't *split* hairs — you know what I meant.
The committee *split* hairs for two hours over one word.

senses.head: Split shares (finance)
senses.body: A company divides each share into several, lowering the price per share.
examples: The stock *split* two for one in June.
The company *has split* its shares three times since 2010.

spread.gloss: To cover or reach a wider area, or to move something out across a surface.

senses.head: Extend over a wider area
senses.body: Of fire, disease, news, and influence. The vowel never changes — *spread* rhymes with *bed* in all three forms, and there is no *spreaded*.
examples: The fire *spread* faster than anyone expected.
The virus *has spread* to eleven counties.
By dawn the oil *had spread* across the whole harbor.

senses.head: Apply something soft to a surface
senses.body: Butter, frosting, glue, mortar. The noun *a spread* is the thing you put on bread.
examples: She *spreads* peanut butter on everything.
*Spread* the frosting while the cake is still warm.
He *spread* butter on both halves.

senses.head: Open something out flat
senses.body: Of blankets, maps, wings, and arms.
examples: *Spread* the blanket over there, in the shade.
They *spread* a map across the hood of the truck.
The bird *had spread* its wings to dry.

senses.head: Pass information around
senses.body: *Spread the word* and *spread a rumor* are both fixed. Often disapproving.
examples: Rumors *spread* through a small town in hours.
Someone *has spread* the news already.
Please don't *spread* this around.

senses.head: Distribute over time or people
senses.body: Usually *spread over* or *spread across*: payments, work, risk.
examples: We *spread* the payments over eighteen months.
The dentist *has spread* the work across three visits.

senses.head: spread out
senses.body: Of people moving apart to cover more ground.
examples: *Spread* out so everyone can see.
The searchers *spread* out along the riverbank.

senses.head: spread oneself too thin
senses.body: Fixed idiom: take on so much that nothing gets proper attention.
examples: She *has spread* herself too thin this semester.
He *spread* himself too thin and finished nothing.

sublet.gloss: To rent out to someone else a place you are renting yourself.

senses.head: Rent out your rental
senses.body: Forms come from *let* in its "rent out" sense — no *subletted*. The noun pulls the stress forward: *a summer SUB-let*.
examples: Many students *sublet* their apartments over the summer.
He *sublet* his studio to a friend while he was in Chicago.
She *has sublet* the same one-bedroom three years running.
My lease says I can't *sublet* at all.

senses.head: Take a place on a sublease
senses.body: Speakers use the verb in both directions; only context tells you who is renting from whom.
examples: We *sublet* a place near campus for three months last fall.
They *had sublet* the unit from a graduate student who never told the landlord.

senses.head: Subcontract work
senses.body: Chiefly British construction usage; Americans say *subcontract* or *sub out*.
examples: The builder *sublets* the electrical work.
Most of the finish work *had been sublet* to a smaller firm.

sweat.gloss: To give off moisture through the skin, and by extension to worry or to work very hard.

senses.head: Perspire
senses.body: American writing prefers the invariant *sweat*, British writing *sweated*; both are standard. The vowel rhymes with *bet*, not *beat*.
examples: I *sweat* buckets on that hike last August.
He *sweats* through a shirt just walking to the subway.
The pitcher *had sweat* right through his cap by the fourth inning.

senses.head: Worry, be anxious
senses.body: Most often in the fixed negatives *don't sweat it* and *don't sweat the small stuff*.
examples: Don't *sweat* the small stuff.
She *has sweat* over this presentation for a week.

senses.head: Work very hard
senses.body: Usually *sweat over* something, or the fixed *sweat blood*.
examples: They *sweated* over that budget for a month.
He *has sweat* blood for this company.

senses.head: sweat it out
senses.body: Wait through something unpleasant with no way to speed it up.
examples: We had to *sweat* it out until the results came back.
We *sweated* out the last ten minutes of the game.

senses.head: Give off moisture (of things)
senses.body: Of a cold glass, a block of cheese, or a basement wall in humid weather.
examples: The glass *sweats* in this humidity.
The basement walls *had sweat* all through July.

senses.head: Cook gently in fat
senses.body: Cooking term: cook vegetables soft over low heat without letting them brown.
examples: *Sweat* the onions in butter for about five minutes.
He *sweated* the leeks before adding the stock.

senses.head: Broadcast on television
senses.body: A dated word — American English now says *broadcast*, *air*, or *televise*. Forms follow *cast*, so never *telecasted*.
examples: CBS *telecasts* the tournament every April.
The network *telecast* the moon landing to sixty countries.
The game *has been telecast* in prime time twice this season.
The ceremony *had been telecast* live before the tape was lost.
They will *telecast* the final round on Sunday.

thrust.gloss: To push something forward suddenly and hard, or to force someone into a situation.

senses.head: Push forcefully
senses.body: The literal sense, always sudden and usually with a direction word: *into*, *forward*, *out*. No *thrusted* in careful writing.
examples: He *thrust* his hands into his pockets and said nothing.
She *thrusts* her chin out whenever she is challenged.
Don't *thrust* the pole any deeper — you'll hit the line.

senses.head: Force into a role (passive)
senses.body: *be thrust into* is the commonest frame in modern prose, and it always implies the person did not choose it.
examples: The accident *has thrust* the mayor into a fight she never wanted.
History *had thrust* an ordinary man into an impossible job.
She was *thrust* into the lead role two days before opening.

senses.head: Force something on someone
senses.body: *thrust something on* or *upon someone* — slightly formal, always unwelcome.
examples: They *thrust* the job on him and then complained about how he did it.
No one should have that kind of responsibility *thrust* upon them at nineteen.

senses.head: Stab, lunge
senses.body: Fencing and hand-to-hand combat, and the source of the noun *a thrust*.
examples: He *thrust* the blade forward and missed.
The two fencers *have thrust* and parried for an hour.

senses.head: Jut out, protrude
senses.body: Of cliffs, piers, and towers — the shape of a sudden push, held still.
examples: A rock ledge *thrusts* out over the valley.
The pier *thrust* two hundred feet into the lake.

typecast.gloss: To keep casting an actor in the same kind of role, or to label a person by one trait.

senses.head: Cast in the same kind of role
senses.ru: утверждать на однотипные роли, эксплуатировать типаж
senses.body: Nearly always passive: *he was typecast as the villain*. Forms follow *cast*; *typecasted* is not standard.
examples: Hollywood *typecasts* character actors within about two films.
That single role *typecast* him for twenty years.
She *has been typecast* as the tough boss in every series since.

senses.head: Pigeonhole a person
senses.body: Outside acting: judge someone by one visible trait or one job they once had.
examples: It is hard not to *typecast* someone you have only seen in one job.
The industry *had typecast* him long before he noticed.

undercut.gloss: To sell more cheaply than a rival, or to weaken something from underneath.

senses.head: Sell below a competitor
senses.body: Business. The verb is stressed un-dur-KUT; the noun *an UN-dur-cut* moves the stress forward.
examples: Their online store *undercuts* every shop in town.
The importer *undercut* local growers by thirty percent.
Cheap imports *have undercut* the whole industry.

senses.head: Weaken, undermine
senses.body: Figurative: take the support out from under an argument, a policy, or a person.
examples: His own memo *has undercut* everything he said in the meeting.
Two earlier rulings *had undercut* the state's argument.
Don't *undercut* your own case with a joke.

senses.head: Cut away from underneath
senses.body: Literal, in carpentry, masonry, and geology — a river undercuts a bank until it collapses.
examples: The river *had undercut* the bank until the tree fell in.
The mason *undercuts* the joint so the mortar holds.

uppercut.gloss: To hit someone with a short upward punch from below.

senses.head: Punch upward from below
senses.body: Boxing shorthand. The noun — *a left uppercut* — is far commoner than the verb. Forms follow *cut*.
examples: He *uppercuts* whenever his opponent drops a shoulder.
She *uppercut* him twice in the final round.
The champion *has uppercut* his way out of trouble before.
By the eighth the challenger *had uppercut* him into the ropes.
You can't *uppercut* from that far away.

upset.gloss: To make someone unhappy, to knock something over, or to beat a favorite.

senses.head: Make someone unhappy
senses.body: The everyday sense. The participle doubles as an adjective — *he looked upset* — and is stressed up-SET, while the noun *an UP-set* moves the stress forward.
examples: It *upsets* her when people are late.
The email *upset* him more than he let on.
Try not to *upset* the baby right before a nap.

senses.head: Disturb the stomach
senses.body: Fixed collocation: *upset someone's stomach*, and the adjective *an upset stomach*.
examples: Rich food *has upset* my stomach all week.
The medication *upset* his stomach for two days.

senses.head: Knock something over
senses.body: The oldest sense and still current, though *knock over* is commoner in speech.
examples: He *upset* an entire tray of glasses.
The cat *has upset* the water bowl twice today.
Careful — you'll *upset* the whole board.

senses.head: Beat a favorite
senses.body: Sports and politics. The noun is even commoner: *a major upset*.
examples: A tenth seed *had upset* the champion in the first round.
An unknown candidate *upset* the incumbent by four points.

senses.head: Disrupt a plan or balance
senses.body: Of schedules, ecosystems, and settled arrangements.
examples: The strike *upset* our whole delivery schedule.
One late shipment can *upset* the balance for a month.
The ruling *has upset* decades of settled practice.

wed.gloss: To marry someone, to perform a marriage, or to join two things closely together.

senses.head: Marry, get married
senses.body: Formal or headline English — *Couple weds after 40 years*. In plain speech Americans say *get married*. Both *wed* and *wedded* are standard pasts.
examples: They *wed* in a courthouse ceremony last fall.
The couple *weds* on Saturday.
By then he *had wed* twice and divorced once.
They plan to *wed* in the spring.

senses.head: Perform a marriage
senses.body: Transitive, with the officiant as the subject: a judge or minister *weds* the couple.
examples: The same judge *wed* both of my sisters.
A retired chaplain *has wedded* half the couples in that town.

senses.head: Join two things closely
senses.body: Figurative and a little literary: *wed X to Y*, of styles, ideas, or qualities.
examples: A good design *weds* comfort to durability.
The album *wedded* country lyrics to a punk rhythm section.

senses.head: be wedded to an idea
senses.body: Fixed and mildly critical: too attached to something to give it up. Also *wedded bliss*, where *wedded* is just an adjective.
examples: She *has wedded* herself to a theory the data doesn't support.
He is too *wedded* to the old process to see the problem.

wet.gloss: To make something wet, including the polite way of saying someone urinated.

senses.head: Make something wet
senses.body: American English prefers the invariant *wet*; *wetted* turns up in technical writing (*the wetted surface*) and is the usual British choice.
examples: *Wet* the brush before you load the paint.
Rain *has wet* the whole stack of newspapers.
Someone *had wet* the sponge and left it on the counter.
He *wets* his hair down before every interview.
The technician *wetted* the slide with a drop of saline.

senses.head: Urinate on or in something
senses.body: The polite way to say it: *wet the bed*, *wet oneself*, *wet his pants*.
examples: The toddler *wet* the bed twice last week.
He laughed so hard he nearly *wet* himself.
The puppy *has wet* the rug again.

senses.head: wet one's whistle
senses.body: A dated, jokey idiom for having a drink.
examples: They stopped at a tavern to *wet* their whistles.
He *had wet* his whistle before the speech, and it showed.
